newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Hong Kong media admit to self-censorship on China.
newsitem.headline: Hong Kong media admit to self-censorship on China.

text.p: One in five Hong Kong journalists said in a survey they hesitated before criticising the Chinese government but they suspected more than half their colleagues were guilty of the same self-censorship.

"Since self-censorship is seen as professionally dishonourable, most journalists tend to think of themselves as more outspoken than their colleagues," the survey's authors at the Chinese University of Hong Kong said.

Half of those surveyed agreed that most journalists hesitate to criticise the Chinese government. One third thought that most journalists also tempered their criticism of large corporations in Hong Kong.
Only 20.1 percent admitted that they themselves hesitated to criticise the Chinese government, while only 12.5 percent said they hesitated to criticise Hong Kong corporations.

Conducted as part of the university's "Mass Media and Political Transition" project, the survey, released this week, questioned 553 journalists working during the territory's July 1 transition to Chinese rule.
More than 150 years of British rule in Hong Kong will end at midnight on June 30.

The figures in the latest survey are lower than those in one conducted by the Hong Kong Journalists Association in 1995, which revealed that 90 percent of journalists surveyed believed self-censorship was occurring in Hong Kong.

"It should be noted, however, more than half (52.3 percent) worry that press freedom of Hong Kong will be affected after 1997. One-third (32 percent) take a 'neutral' attitude on the issue," the latest survey said.

Half of those who participated in the new survey adopted a neutral stance on the likelihood that the "one country, two systems" policy guiding Hong Kong's return to China would work, while slightly more than half believed Hong Kong's future "is becoming better and better."
"These large proportions of 'neutral' answers may be seen as journalists taking a 'wait and see' attitude towards Hong Kong's uncertain future," the survey's authors wrote.

Eight in 10 journalists (81.9 percent) objected to the statement: "In order to maintain stability and prosperity during the transition, journalists should not expose too much (of the) dark side of the society."
"In sum, although Hong Kong journalists highly support the values of press freedom, they (seemed) to develop considerable uncertainty about Hong Kong's future," the survey's authors wrote.
